I’ve just kicked off the full‑pipeline end‑to‑end test with a generous 30‑minute timeout, launching it in the background (task ID b2btb0hd1). The test is still running, and I need to know when it finishes and what its final output looks like before I can decide whether the recent change (updating the hard‑coded model‑parameter count) resolved the failure.

Because the background command is still active, I can’t simply read the output file immediately; it will be incomplete and may even be empty at this point. I also can’t block the assistant with a long‑running `sleep` or a direct `wait` on the process, as the environment enforces limits on chained sleeps and long‑running synchronous commands. The safest approach is to poll for the presence of the pytest process and only once it has terminated should I pull the tail of the log.

To do this, I’ll use a `pgrep -f "pytest tests/e2e/test_train_entry"` check inside an `until` loop that repeats every 15 seconds. The loop condition `! pgrep …` will become true when the process no longer exists, at which point the loop exits. After the loop, I’ll `tail -3` the output file associated with the background task to capture the final few lines (which typically contain the summary and any error messages). I’ll also pipe through `tr '\\r' '\\n'` to normalize line endings, then another `tail -3` to ensure I only get the last three lines after the transformation.

Since this whole waiting construct could still take several minutes, I’ll request it be run in the background as well (`run_in_background: true`). That way the assistant remains responsive and can later read the result once the background task completes. This aligns with the platform’s guidance to avoid long blocking calls and to monitor long‑running processes via background tasks.

Thus, the next step is to issue a Bash tool call that implements this waiting‑and‑tailing logic, with `run_in_background` set so the assistant can continue after scheduling it.
